role.altitude: The detective keeps investigating, judging what is missing, writing official reports in their own words and securing scenes; linking persons by hand, checking reports against checklists and copying scene notes shrink a little.
skills_to_grow: Keeping offence checklists and case links clean so gaps show early
role.ambitious_version: A detective who sees on day one which elements of the offence still lack evidence.

tasks.short: Record progress of the investigation in official reports, maintain informational files on suspects, keep the case log, draft warrant requests, have them reviewed and submit them to the prosecutor or magistrate.

steps.what: Detective records progress of the investigation in official reports of each action
Detective maintains informational files on suspects: persons, addresses, vehicles and links
Detective keeps the investigation log and task list: in a spreadsheet today; after the change filed reports show as log lines in the case system and the detective writes the tasks
Detective drafts the request with grounds for the magistrate to authorize warrants
Team leader reviews and approves the final warrant request
Detective checks the final request as approved: grounds, persons and addresses, and the prosecutor or magistrate it goes to
Detective submits the approved request to the prosecutor or magistrate

approvals.approved_version: The warrant request exactly as approved by the team leader in s5 and checked by the detective in s5c, submitted once to the prosecutor or magistrate named in it; any change goes back for approval and a new check.

tasks.design: Official reports keep being written by the detective, with templates per action type that fill case number, times and persons from the case file; no model drafts reports, because the digest's trial found no time saved and police data may not go into general model tools. In the case system, fixed matching links persons, addresses and vehicles mentioned in reports to existing records, and the detective confirms each link. The task list lives in the case system instead of a spreadsheet, and each filed report shows there as a log line, so actions are not copied into the log. Warrant requests stay the detective's work, approved by the team leader and checked once more by the detective before submission.
tasks.previous_blocker: Links between persons and the task list were kept by hand beside the case system.
tasks.enabler_now: Case systems with entity matching and task lists.
tasks.still_hard: Writing grounds for a warrant that hold up.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing which detail will convince the magistrate.
tasks.altitude: A little less administration; reports and requests stay the detective's own.

reach.learn: Whether confirmed links save the analyst rework.

evidence.claim: In a randomised trial, AI-drafted patrol reports were not written faster; one department claimed 8 against 23 minutes.
The police's own language model runs on police servers but is not for police data under the police data act.
Automated decisions with adverse effect need human intervention; high-risk processing needs a DPIA.

assumptions: Boundary: recording the case and requesting warrants; the magistrate's decision is outside.

Input contract for s2: persons, addresses and vehicles already in the police registration system, matched by fixed rules on names, dates of birth, addresses and plates; the detective confirms every link.

Warrant requests, the approval and the final check keep their full time; s1 keeps 90 because templates fill case number, times and persons and the detective writes the report; s2 keeps 70 because links are proposed and confirming them stays; s3 keeps 80 because log lines come from filed reports and tasks are still written. Team leader time is outside the detective's savings.
unknowns: How many links per case need checking.
research_questions: Do wrong links between persons fall?

already_counted.description: Detective confirms or rejects proposed links between persons and records.

incremental.description: Detective keeps report templates current with the team.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: names and addresses are often spelled differently, so few links are proposed, and templates fill little (6.8); high: links and templates work as designed (12.8).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Read completed police reports, check them against the elements of the offence, analyze what additional information and investigative work is needed, and set the tasks for the team.

steps.what: Detective reads the completed police reports in the case

loop.input: The reports in the case file, on police servers only.
loop.output: Each sentence tagged by topic and the documents ordered by topic.
loop.check: Code checks that every source sentence appears once in the ordered view and that nothing is summarised or left out. The detective reads every source document in full and re-tags any sentence whose topic tag does not match what it says.
loop.stop: One tagging run per new batch of reports.
loop.why_not_simpler: Keyword search misses the same fact written in different words.

steps.what: Detective checks the reports against the elements of the offence and required evidence; after the change the checklist shows which elements have filled fields and the detective reads the evidence behind each one
Detective analyzes and decides what additional information and investigative work is needed
Detective writes the tasks for the team: in a spreadsheet sent round today, in the case system where the team sees them after the change

tasks.design: A tagging step on police servers marks sentences in the case reports by topic and orders the documents, without summarising, so the detective reads the case in a useful order. A rule-based checklist per offence type lists the elements and evidence usually needed and shows which ones the structured report fields already cover; a filled field is not taken as proof, so the detective reads the evidence behind each element. Deciding what more is needed stays with the detective, and the chosen tasks are created in the case system for the team.
tasks.previous_blocker: Gaps were found by reading every report against one's own memory of what is needed.
tasks.enabler_now: Police tagging of case documents and rule-based checklists already in police use.
tasks.still_hard: Gaps that only show when the story does not add up.
tasks.human_edge: Sensing that a witness statement is too neat.
tasks.altitude: Less searching through reports; investigative judgement stays.

reach.learn: Whether files arrive with fewer missing elements.

evidence.claim: A police tool tags sentences by topic and orders documents; summarising was rejected because details matter.
A police tool asks fraud victims for missing facts using argumentation rules, not a language model.
AI that assesses the reliability of evidence is an AI Act high-risk use; tagging and checklists do not assess it.

assumptions: Boundary: analysing completed reports to plan further work; doing the work is outside.
Input contract for s1: reports in the case system on police servers; no data leave police systems.
Input contract for s2: checklists per offence type kept by the team's legal adviser; structured report fields filled by reporting officers as today.

Deciding further work keeps its full time. s1 keeps 90 because the detective still reads every document and only the order saves searching; s2 keeps 75 because the checklist lists the elements and the detective still weighs the evidence for each; s4 keeps 85 because the spreadsheet is no longer sent round and the tasks are still written.
unknowns: How often checklists cover the offence types handled.
research_questions: Do prosecutors return fewer files for more investigation?

already_counted.description: Detective checks flagged checklist gaps against the reports.

incremental.description: Detective suggests checklist changes to the legal adviser.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: most cases are small, so ordering saves no reading and structured fields are often empty (4.4); high: larger files with filled fields (11.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Note and mark objects found such as footprints, tire tracks, bullets and bloodstains, photograph their location, take measurements of the scene and keep the scene log.

steps.what: Detective notes and marks objects found with numbered markers
Detective photographs the location of objects and the scene
Detective takes measurements of the scene: positions and distances
Detective lists markers, photo numbers and measurements in the scene log: copied by hand today; after the change the scene app pairs them and the detective checks the pairing
Detective writes the description of each marked object in the scene log

tasks.design: Marking and photographing stay with the detective. A scene app on a police device records each marker number with the photos taken of it, their time and position, and the readings of a laser distance meter paired to it, so the scene log builds itself while the detective adds descriptions. Originals are stored unaltered with a checksum for the chain of evidence. Large scenes are still measured by forensic investigators.
tasks.previous_blocker: Photo numbers and measurements were written on paper and matched up afterwards.
tasks.enabler_now: Scene apps that tie photos and laser measurements to marker numbers.
tasks.still_hard: Deciding what at a scene is evidence.
tasks.human_edge: Noticing the trace nobody else saw.
tasks.altitude: Less writing at the scene; finding evidence stays.

reach.learn: Whether detectives' scene logs need less rework.

evidence.claim: Camera apps record time and position with each photo, and laser distance meters pair to phones.
Police data are kept only as long as the police data act allows.

assumptions: Boundary: recording objects at a scene; forensic processing is outside.
Input contract for s4: marker numbers entered by the detective and photos and measurements captured by the app during s2 and s3.

Coverage: the app is used at about 70% of scenes; at the rest, paper logs continue. s4b keeps 40: 30 for scenes without the app and 10 for checking the pairing. Descriptions (s4) are a first record and keep their full time.
Marking and photographing keep their full time.
unknowns: How often detectives record scenes without forensic investigators.
research_questions: Do scene logs have fewer mismatches between photos and markers?

incremental.description: No ongoing upkeep: checking the app's marker and photo pairing is kept in s4b.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: the app is used at only about half of scenes (12.3); high: about 70% of scenes as assumed (14.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Cordon off the scene, secure the deceased body and obtain evidence from it, prevent bystanders from tampering prior to the medical examiner's arrival, keep the entry log and brief the medical examiner.

steps.what: Detective cordons off the scene and prevents bystanders from tampering
Detective guards the deceased body at the scene
Detective keeps the log of who enters the scene: names and times on a paper list today; after the change police cards are scanned and others are typed
Detective secures and obtains evidence from the body under forensic guidance
Detective briefs the medical examiner on arrival

tasks.design: Securing the scene and the body stays fully in person. The only change: the entry log is kept on the police device, where scanning a colleague's police card or typing a name records the time in and out, instead of a paper list.
tasks.previous_blocker: Nothing blocked it; this is scene work.
tasks.enabler_now: Mobile entry logs that scan service cards.
tasks.human_edge: Keeping a scene intact while dealing with grieving family.

reach.learn: Whether a complete entry log answers contamination questions.

evidence.claim: Mobile logs can record entries by scanning cards.
Logs of staff entries could monitor colleagues and need works council consent if used for that.

assumptions: Boundary: from arrival to the medical examiner taking over; the post-mortem is outside.
Input contract for s2: police cards of colleagues scanned at the cordon; others are typed by the detective.
Cordoning, guarding the body, evidence and briefing keep their full time. The entry log keeps 40 for scanning cards and typing people who carry no police card.
research_questions: Is the entry log complete more often?

incremental.description: Detective checks the entry log before handing over the scene.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: most people entering are from other services without police cards, so names are typed (2.2); high: most entrants are police with cards (4.6).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional
